questions.question: In two or three sentences: what problem are you solving, and for whom?
questions.why: Every feature must trace back to a real user need. A clear problem statement is the yardstick used later to accept or reject scope.
questions.example: Small clinics lose revenue to missed appointments; we want a booking and reminder tool they can set up in a day.

questions.question: Who are the users and roles (for example customer, staff, admin), and what are the 3-5 most important things each one must be able to do?
questions.why: Roles drive authorization rules, screens, and test scenarios. User journeys become the end-to-end and regression tests that protect working functionality.
questions.example: Patient: find a slot, book, cancel. Receptionist: see the day's schedule, rebook. Admin: manage staff accounts.

questions.question: How will you know the product is succeeding? Give 1-3 measurable goals with a time frame.
questions.why: Measurable goals let the team prioritize and tell the difference between finished and merely busy.
questions.example: 30 active clinics within 90 days; no-show rate reduced by 20%.

questions.question: Which platforms must MVP 1 support?
questions.why: Each additional platform multiplies build, test, and release effort. Starting narrow keeps quality high.

options.label: Responsive web only
options.tradeoff: Fastest and cheapest; one codebase; works on phones through the browser. No app-store presence or deep device features.

options.label: Responsive web + installable PWA
options.tradeoff: Adds home-screen install and basic offline support at modest cost; limited access to some device features.

options.label: Web + native or cross-platform mobile app
options.tradeoff: Best device integration and store presence; roughly doubles testing and release work and needs app-store processes.

questions.question: List the functions MVP 1 needs and any external systems it must connect to (payments, email/SMS, maps, identity, accounting, and so on).
questions.why: Integrations are the most common source of hidden effort, cost, security risk, and failure modes.
questions.example: Booking calendar, SMS reminders (provider X), card payments (provider Y).

questions.question: Which features are must-haves for MVP 1? Keep it to the smallest set that delivers the core user value.
questions.why: A small MVP ships sooner, gets real feedback sooner, and is easier to build correctly. Anything not listed is out of scope until approved.
questions.example: FEAT-001 book appointment; FEAT-002 cancel appointment; FEAT-003 SMS reminder.

questions.question: What is explicitly NOT in MVP 1 (non-goals), and what are the candidates for MVP 2?
questions.why: Writing non-goals down is the cheapest protection against scope creep, including AI-suggested extras.
questions.example: Non-goals: multi-language UI, reporting dashboards. MVP 2 candidates: waiting list, online payments.

questions.question: How many users do you expect in the first 6-12 months (and at peak at the same time)?
questions.why: Expected load decides whether simple infrastructure is enough and sets the measurable triggers for scaling work.

options.label: Under 100 users; a few concurrent
options.tradeoff: Single small instance is fine; minimal cost; avoid over-engineering.

options.label: Hundreds to a few thousand users; tens of concurrent
options.tradeoff: Standard managed hosting with a managed database and basic caching/pagination is sufficient.

options.label: Tens of thousands or more; hundreds+ concurrent
options.tradeoff: Needs load testing, capacity planning, and possibly queues/caching from the start; higher cost and complexity.

options.label: Unknown
options.tradeoff: Treated as option B with explicit review triggers (latency, CPU, database load) that prompt re-evaluation.

questions.question: How available must the system be for its most critical workflow?
questions.why: Availability targets drive cost: each extra 'nine' usually means redundancy, more operations work, and stricter release practices.

options.label: Best effort during business hours
options.tradeoff: Cheapest; acceptable for internal tools and early prototypes.

options.label: 99.5% monthly (about 3.6 hours downtime per month)
options.tradeoff: Reasonable for most MVPs; needs monitoring, tested rollback, and backups.

options.label: 99.9% monthly (about 43 minutes per month)
options.tradeoff: Needs redundancy, automated alerts, on-call practice, and zero-downtime deploys.

options.label: 99.95% or higher
options.tradeoff: Multi-zone design and mature operations; costly. Rarely justified for an MVP.

questions.question: If the system or its data is lost, how much data loss (RPO) and how long an outage (RTO) can the business tolerate?
questions.why: These numbers decide backup frequency, restore drills, and whether replicas are needed.

options.label: RPO 24 hours / RTO 8 hours
options.tradeoff: Daily backups with a rehearsed restore; low cost.

options.label: RPO 1 hour / RTO 4 hours
options.tradeoff: Point-in-time recovery and a documented, drilled restore; moderate cost.

options.label: RPO 15 minutes or less / RTO 1 hour or less
options.tradeoff: Continuous replication and automated failover; high cost and complexity.

questions.question: What is the most sensitive data the product will hold?
questions.why: Data sensitivity sets the security baseline, legal obligations (for example privacy law), encryption, retention, and audit needs.

options.label: No personal data
options.tradeoff: Lightest security and privacy workload.

options.label: Personal data (names, emails, phone numbers)
options.tradeoff: Needs data minimization, retention/deletion rules, encryption in transit and at rest, access logging.

options.label: Regulated data (payments, health, children, financial)
options.tradeoff: Needs formal threat modeling, compliance review, strict access control, audit trails, often a specialist advisor. Prefer certified third parties (e.g. a payment provider) over handling the data yourself.

questions.question: Which architecture style should MVP 1 use? (Explicit microservices decision.)
questions.why: This is the most expensive decision to reverse. Microservices give independent deployment and scaling, but add network failure modes, distributed data consistency, and operational load that small teams often cannot afford at MVP stage.

options.label: Monolith
options.tradeoff: Simplest to build and run. Risk: boundaries erode over time unless enforced.

options.label: Modular monolith
options.tradeoff: One deployable with enforced module boundaries and module-owned data. Simple operations now; modules can later be extracted if triggers are met (not effortless).

options.label: Microservices from the beginning
options.tradeoff: Justified only by independent deployment, separate team ownership, very different scaling profiles, or isolation needs; requires mature operations (observability, CI/CD per service, contract testing).

options.label: Other (explain)
options.tradeoff: For example serverless or event-driven; needs an ADR justifying it against requirements.

questions.question: Which technology stack should the application use?
questions.why: The best stack is usually the one your team and AI assistants can build, test, and operate reliably. Familiarity reduces defects.

options.label: The stack the team already knows best (specify)
options.tradeoff: Lowest risk and fastest start; confirm it has mature tooling for testing and security.

options.label: TypeScript end-to-end
options.tradeoff: One language for web and server; large ecosystem; strong AI-assistant support.

options.label: Python backend + TypeScript frontend
options.tradeoff: Strong for data/ML-heavy products; two toolchains to maintain.

options.label: Other (specify)
options.tradeoff: Record the reason and the plan to cover tooling gaps.

questions.question: Where will it be hosted, and which database type fits?
questions.why: Hosting choice sets operating effort, cost, and how easily you can scale or recover. Managed services trade some control for far less operations work.

options.label: Managed platform (PaaS) + managed relational database
options.tradeoff: Least operations effort; automated backups and patches; some vendor lock-in.

options.label: Managed containers on a cloud provider + managed database
options.tradeoff: More control and portability; more configuration to own.

options.label: Kubernetes
options.tradeoff: Maximum flexibility; significant expertise and operations cost; rarely justified for an MVP.

options.label: Self-hosted / on-premises
options.tradeoff: Required by some compliance cases; you own patching, backups, and availability.

questions.question: What are your team size, each person's experience level (beginner/intermediate/senior), MVP 1 target date, and monthly infrastructure budget?
questions.why: These constraints shape how much guidance, review, and automation the team needs, and what is realistic to build.
questions.example: 6 developers (2 senior, 2 intermediate, 2 beginner); MVP 1 in 12 weeks; infrastructure budget 300 per month.

questions.question: How will users sign in and how will permissions be controlled?
questions.why: Authentication and authorization are the most security-critical parts of most products and are easy to get subtly wrong.

options.label: Managed identity provider (hosted login, MFA, social login) + role-based access control
options.tradeoff: Strongest security for the least effort; ongoing per-user cost and vendor dependency.

options.label: Built-in email/password with a vetted framework library
options.tradeoff: Full control; you own password storage, reset flows, MFA, and abuse protection.

options.label: Enterprise SSO (SAML/OIDC) for business customers
options.tradeoff: Required by many B2B buyers; more integration and support effort.

options.label: No sign-in (public content only)
options.tradeoff: Only valid if there is no user-specific data.

questions.question: How will API contracts and data ownership be defined?
questions.why: Clear contracts and one owner per dataset are what keep parallel developers and AI agents from breaking each other's work.

options.label: Contract-first (OpenAPI/JSON Schema) and each module owns its tables
options.tradeoff: Best protection against accidental breaking changes; small up-front effort.

options.label: Code-first with a generated contract, each module owns its tables
options.tradeoff: Quicker to start; the generated contract must be checked in and diffed in CI.

options.label: Other (specify)
options.tradeoff: For example GraphQL schema-first or event schemas; record in an ADR.

questions.question: How rigorous should testing be for MVP 1?
questions.why: Testing is what stops regressions. Rigor should match the cost of failure.

options.label: Standard: unit + integration + end-to-end for critical journeys, run automatically on every pull request
options.tradeoff: Recommended baseline for a team using AI assistants.

options.label: Strict: Standard plus contract, load, and security tests before every release
options.tradeoff: For regulated or high-availability products; slower pipeline and more upkeep.

options.label: Lean: unit tests and a manual smoke test
options.tradeoff: Only for throwaway prototypes; not recommended for anything customers will rely on.

questions.question: Which repository platform will you use?
questions.why: Branch protection, code owners, and CI configuration are platform-specific. The kit's automation targets GitHub.

options.label: GitHub
options.tradeoff: Kit works as-is (workflows, CODEOWNERS, templates, protection script).

options.label: GitLab / Azure DevOps / Bitbucket
options.tradeoff: Scripts under scripts/ are portable; CI files, CODEOWNERS format, and protection setup must be translated and re-verified.

questions.question: Who is the Technical Owner (architecture and security decisions) and who are the Release Approvers? Name people, and a backup for each.
questions.why: Human accountability requires named people. AI can recommend, but cannot approve its own high-risk decisions or production releases.
questions.example: Technical Owner: Asha (backup Ben). Release Approvers: Asha, Chen.

questions.question: What review policy should pull requests follow?
questions.why: Review is the main human control over AI-generated changes.

options.label: 1 approving review + code-owner approval on owned paths
options.tradeoff: Good balance for up to 10 developers; fast but safe.

options.label: 2 approvals on shared/high-risk paths, 1 elsewhere
options.tradeoff: Stronger control for shared components, schemas, and security code; slower merges on those paths.

options.label: Pairing/mobbing plus 1 approving review
options.tradeoff: Best for upskilling beginners; costs developer time.

questions.question: Which environment flow will you use?
questions.why: Environments let you find problems before customers do. Each extra environment costs money and upkeep.

options.label: Dev -> QA -> Staging -> Production
options.tradeoff: Recommended standard; one immutable build is promoted through all four.

options.label: Dev -> Staging -> Production (QA folded into Staging)
options.tradeoff: Cheaper for very small teams; QA and release rehearsal compete for one environment.

questions.question: How should deployments be rolled back if something goes wrong?
questions.why: A rehearsed rollback turns an outage into a short incident.

options.label: Redeploy the previous immutable build (database changes must be backward-compatible)
options.tradeoff: Simple and reliable; requires disciplined migrations.

options.label: Blue/green deployment
options.tradeoff: Near-instant switch back; doubles production capacity during release.

options.label: Canary/progressive rollout
options.tradeoff: Limits blast radius; needs strong monitoring. Add only when scale justifies it.

questions.question: What level of monitoring and incident response do you want at launch?
questions.why: You cannot fix what you cannot see. The baseline is cheap and prevents long undetected outages.

options.label: Baseline: structured logs, uptime check, error tracking, alerts to a named on-call person
options.tradeoff: Recommended minimum for production.

options.label: Full: baseline plus metrics, tracing, dashboards, and SLO-based alerts
options.tradeoff: Needed for tight availability targets or microservices; more setup and cost.

options.label: Minimal: uptime check only
options.tradeoff: Only for internal or pre-launch use.

questions.question: How will you control cost and plan long-term maintenance?
questions.why: Unwatched cloud spend and unmaintained dependencies are common slow-burning failures. Right-sizing also reduces energy use.

options.label: Monthly budget alert and cost review; monthly dependency updates; quarterly technical-debt review
options.tradeoff: Light routine that prevents surprises.

options.label: Quarterly reviews only
options.tradeoff: Less effort; slower to catch cost spikes and vulnerable dependencies.
